note_rewrites.desert-monasticism--iconophile-byzantine: Basil of Caesarea wrote that he found many monks in Alexandria and the rest of Egypt. In 787 the Second Council of Nicaea told double monasteries to keep Basil's rule. Its acts record images of 'the fathers and cultivators of the desert', but no text we hold shows iconophile monks drawing on Egypt directly.
note_rewrites.desert-monasticism--insular-irish-monast: An eighth-century Irish monk on the Continent, mixing fact with legend, traced the Irish daily office to Antony, Paul, Macarius and other early hermits. Warren, who edited the Bangor Antiphonary in 1895, judged this single late account sound at its core but wrong in detail. He held that any Eastern features reached Ireland through Gaul.
note_rewrites.gallic-monastic-ascetic-christianity--in: A single eighth-century Irish account names Cassian and the monks of Lérins as links in the chain that reached Ireland. Beyond that, there is only Patrick's own wish, in his Confession, to visit the brethren in Gaul. Warren, the 1895 editor of the Bangor Antiphonary, held that Ireland's Eastern features came through Gaul.
note_rewrites.the-waldensians--waldensians-in-the-alps: Bernard Gui, an inquisitor writing in the 1320s, says the Waldensians' first error, contempt for church authority, still continues. His editor adds that Gui's prosecutions drove Waldensians into the Alps of Dauphiné and northern Italy. The same movement carried on in the Alps after 1300.
note_rewrites.imperial-juridical-christianity--donatis: Emperor Constantine granted the Donatists judges, who heard their case at Rome with Miltiades, the city's bishop. Optatus, a Catholic bishop, reports that a Donatist bishop then appealed. Constantine replied: 'Oh, mad daring of their fury!'
note_rewrites.donatism--imperial-juridical-christianit: Optatus says that agents of Emperor Constans, Paul and Macarius, came to Donatus. Donatus burst out: 'What has the Emperor to do with the Church?' Optatus opposed Donatus, so this is a hostile report.
note_rewrites.lollardy--the-hussite-and-bohemian-breth: The English editor of Hus's On the Church reports that Hus took paragraph after paragraph from Wyclif's treatise on the same subject. On 6 July the Council of Constance condemned Wyclif's errors and sentenced Hus the same day. Wyclif's teaching began Lollardy, but this shows his influence on Hus, not that English Lollard communities shaped the Bohemians.
